units.sourceHTML: Control Flow
units.originalInnerHTML: Control Flow

units.sourceHTML: Control flow is used to determine which chunks of code are executed and how many times. Branching statements and expressions decide whether or not to execute some code and looping ones execute something more than once.
units.originalInnerHTML: Control flow is used to determine which chunks of code are executed and how many times. Branching statements and expressions decide whether or not to execute some code and looping ones execute something more than once.

units.sourceHTML: Truth #
units.originalInnerHTML: Truth #

units.sourceHTML: All control flow is based on deciding whether or not to do something. This decision depends on some expression’s value. We take the entire universe of possible objects and divide them into two buckets: some we consider “true” and the rest are “false”. If the expression results in a value in the true bucket, we do one thing. Otherwise, we do something else.
units.originalInnerHTML: All control flow is based on deciding whether or not to do something. This decision depends on some expression’s value. We take the entire universe of possible objects and divide them into two buckets: some we consider “true” and the rest are “false”. If the expression results in a value in the true bucket, we do one thing. Otherwise, we do something else.

units.sourceHTML:

“false”, but what about values of other types? The choice is ultimately
arbitrary, and different languages have different rules. Wren’s rules follow

units.sourceHTML: The boolean value ⟦CODE0⟧ is false.
units.originalInnerHTML: The boolean value false is false.

units.sourceHTML: The null value ⟦CODE0⟧ is false.
units.originalInnerHTML: The null value null is false.

units.sourceHTML: Everything else is true.
units.originalInnerHTML: Everything else is true.

units.sourceHTML:
This means ⟦CODE0⟧, empty strings, and empty collections are all considered “true”
values.

units.sourceHTML: Logical operators #
units.originalInnerHTML: Logical operators #

units.sourceHTML: Unlike most other operators in Wren which are just a special syntax for method calls, the ⟦CODE0⟧ and ⟦CODE1⟧ operators are special. This is because they only conditionally evaluate the right operand—they short-circuit.
units.originalInnerHTML: Unlike most other operators in Wren which are just a special syntax for method calls, the && and || operators are special. This is because they only conditionally evaluate the right operand—they short-circuit.

units.sourceHTML:
A ⟦CODE0⟧ (“logical and”) expression evaluates the left-hand argument. If it’s
false, it returns that value. Otherwise it evaluates and returns the right-hand
argument.
units.originalInnerHTML: A && (“logical and”) expression evaluates the left-hand argument. If it’s false, it returns that value. Otherwise it evaluates and returns the right-hand argument.

units.sourceHTML: A ⟦CODE0⟧ (“logical or”) expression is reversed. If the left-hand argument is true, it’s returned, otherwise the right-hand argument is evaluated and returned:
units.originalInnerHTML: A || (“logical or”) expression is reversed. If the left-hand argument is true, it’s returned, otherwise the right-hand argument is evaluated and returned:

units.sourceHTML:
Also known as the “ternary” operator since it takes three arguments, Wren has
the little “if statement in the form of an expression” you know and love from C
and similar languages.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Also known as the “ternary” operator since it takes three arguments, Wren has
the little “if statement in the form of an expression” you know and love from C
and similar languages.

units.sourceHTML:
It takes a condition expression, followed by ⟦CODE0⟧, followed by a then
expression, a ⟦CODE1⟧, then an else expression. Just like ⟦CODE2⟧, it evaluates the
condition. If true, it evaluates and returns the then expression. Otherwise
it does the else expression.
units.originalInnerHTML: It takes a condition expression, followed by ?, followed by a then expression, a :, then an else expression. Just like if, it evaluates the condition. If true, it evaluates and returns the then expression. Otherwise it does the else expression.

units.sourceHTML: While statements #
units.originalInnerHTML: While statements #

units.sourceHTML:
It’s hard to write a useful program without executing some chunk of code
repeatedly. To do that, you use looping statements. There are two in Wren, and
they should be familiar if you’ve used other imperative languages.

repeatedly. To do that, you use looping statements. There are two in Wren, and
they should be familiar if you’ve used other imperative languages.

units.sourceHTML: A variable name to bind. In the example, that’s ⟦CODE0⟧. Wren will create a new variable with that name whose scope is the body of the loop.

units.sourceHTML: A sequence expression. This determines what you’re looping over. It gets evaluated once before the body of the loop. In this case, it’s a list literal, but it can be any expression.
units.originalInnerHTML: A sequence expression. This determines what you’re looping over. It gets evaluated once before the body of the loop. In this case, it’s a list literal, but it can be any expression.

units.sourceHTML: A body. This is a curly block or a single statement. It gets executed once for each iteration of the loop.

units.sourceHTML: Break statements #
units.originalInnerHTML: Break statements #

units.sourceHTML:
Sometimes, right in the middle of a loop body, you decide you want to bail out
and stop. To do that, you can use a ⟦CODE0⟧ statement. It’s just the ⟦CODE1⟧
keyword all by itself. That immediately exits out of the nearest enclosing
⟦CODE2⟧ or ⟦CODE3⟧ loop.
units.originalInnerHTML: Sometimes, right in the middle of a loop body, you decide you want to bail out and stop. To do that, you can use a break statement. It’s just the break keyword all by itself. That immediately exits out of the nearest enclosing while or for loop.

units.sourceHTML: Continue statements #
units.originalInnerHTML: Continue statements #

units.sourceHTML:
During the execution of a loop body, you might decide that you want to skip the 
rest of this iteration and move on to the next one. You can use a ⟦CODE0⟧ 
statement to do that. It’s just the ⟦CODE1⟧ keyword all by itself. Execution
will immediately jump to the beginning of the next loop iteration (and check the
loop conditions).
units.originalInnerHTML: During the execution of a loop body, you might decide that you want to skip the rest of this iteration and move on to the next one. You can use a continue statement to do that. It’s just the continue keyword all by itself. Execution will immediately jump to the beginning of the next loop iteration (and check the loop conditions).

units.sourceHTML: The iterator protocol #
units.originalInnerHTML: The iterator protocol #

units.sourceHTML:
Lists and ranges cover the two most common kinds of loops, but you should also
be able to define your own sequences. To enable that, the semantics of ⟦CODE0⟧
are defined in terms of an “iterator protocol”. The loop itself doesn’t know
anything about lists or ranges, it just knows how to call two particular
methods on the object that resulted from evaluating the sequence expression.
units.originalInnerHTML: Lists and ranges cover the two most common kinds of loops, but you should also be able to define your own sequences. To enable that, the semantics of for are defined in terms of an “iterator protocol”. The loop itself doesn’t know anything about lists or ranges, it just knows how to call two particular methods on the object that resulted from evaluating the sequence expression.

units.sourceHTML:
First, Wren evaluates the sequence expression and stores it in a hidden
variable (written ⟦CODE0⟧ in the example but in reality it doesn’t have a name
you can use). It also creates a hidden “iterator” variable and initializes it
to ⟦CODE1⟧.
units.originalInnerHTML: First, Wren evaluates the sequence expression and stores it in a hidden variable (written seq_ in the example but in reality it doesn’t have a name you can use). It also creates a hidden “iterator” variable and initializes it to null.

units.sourceHTML: Each iteration, it calls ⟦CODE0⟧ on the sequence, passing in the current iterator value. (In the first iteration, it passes in ⟦CODE1⟧.) The sequence’s job is to take that iterator and advance it to the next element in the sequence. (Or, in the case where the iterator is ⟦CODE2⟧, to advance it to the first element). It then returns either the new iterator, or ⟦CODE3⟧ to indicate that there are no more elements.
units.originalInnerHTML: Each iteration, it calls iterate() on the sequence, passing in the current iterator value. (In the first iteration, it passes in null.) The sequence’s job is to take that iterator and advance it to the next element in the sequence. (Or, in the case where the iterator is null, to advance it to the first element). It then returns either the new iterator, or false to indicate that there are no more elements.

units.sourceHTML:
If ⟦CODE0⟧ is returned, Wren exits out of the loop and we’re done. If anything
else is returned, that means that we have advanced to a new valid element. To
get that, Wren then calls ⟦CODE1⟧ on the sequence and passes in the
iterator value that it just got from calling ⟦CODE2⟧. The sequence uses
that to look up and return the appropriate element.
units.originalInnerHTML: If false is returned, Wren exits out of the loop and we’re done. If anything else is returned, that means that we have advanced to a new valid element. To get that, Wren then calls iteratorValue() on the sequence and passes in the iterator value that it just got from calling iterate(). The sequence uses that to look up and return the appropriate element.

units.sourceHTML: The built-in List and Range types implement ⟦CODE0⟧ and ⟦CODE1⟧ to walk over their respective sequences. You can implement the same methods in your classes to make your own types iterable.
units.originalInnerHTML: The built-in List and Range types implement iterate() and iteratorValue() to walk over their respective sequences. You can implement the same methods in your classes to make your own types iterable.
